procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge (upheld by a Single Judge of the High Court)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 20.04.2023 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in CRLWP No. 4451 of 2022, where a Single Judge disagreed with an earlier Single Judge's order and directed that a charge under s.302 not be framed.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: An initial Single Judge of the High Court upheld an order passed by the Special Judge framing a charge under Section 302 of the Penal Code, 1860. Subsequently, another Single Judge of the High Court disagreed with the earlier order, based on the same set of facts and one trial, and directed that the charge under s.302 not be framed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court held that the subsequent Single Judge, if disagreeing with the earlier order, should have referred the matter to a Division Bench/two-judge Bench instead of passing a conflicting order. The Supreme Court treated the subsequent decision of the Single Judge as one differing with the view expressed in the earlier order and as one referring the matter to a larger bench of two Judges/Division Bench for consideration. The Chief Justice of the High Court was requested to constitute an appropriate Bench. The impugned judgment/order was partly set aside, and the appeal was allowed and disposed of. The Supreme Court clarified that it did not express any opinion on the merits of the case.

directions: The impugned judgment/order is accordingly partly set aside.
We clarify we have not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Single Judge of the High Court can disagree with an earlier order of a Single Judge based on the same set of facts and one trial, and give a conflicting order.

facts: A Single Judge of the High Court upheld a trial court's decision to frame a charge under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. This order became final as it was not challenged.
Subsequently, another Single Judge of the same High Court, dealing with the same set of facts and the same trial, disagreed with the first order.
This second judge issued a conflicting order, directing that the charge under Section 302 should not be framed.
This created an "incongruous situation" with two contradictory orders from coordinate benches arising from a single trial.
law: The Supreme Court emphasized the principles of judicial propriety, decorum, and discipline.
It cited the rule that if a Single Judge disagrees with a prior decision of another Single Judge (a coordinate bench), they should not simply pass a conflicting order.
The proper judicial procedure is to refer the matter to a larger bench, such as a Division Bench of two judges, for reconsideration.
The Court referenced Rule 8 of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960, which allows a judge to report to the Chief Justice if a matter could be more advantageously heard by a larger bench.
application: The Court applied the principle of judicial discipline to the facts, stating that the second Single Judge, upon disagreeing with the first order, should have referred the matter to a Division Bench instead of passing a conflicting judgment.
By issuing a contrary order, the second judge acted against established judicial practice and created an untenable situation with two opposing directives in the same case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court resolved the issue by deciding to treat the second, conflicting order not as a final decision, but as an order of reference to a larger bench. It directed that the second judge's order be considered as one expressing disagreement with the earlier order and referring the matter for consideration by a Division Bench. The Court then requested the Chief Justice of the High Court to constitute an appropriate bench to hear and resolve the conflicting views.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Single Judge of the High Court can disagree with an earlier order of a Single Judge based on the same set of facts and one trial, and give a conflicting order.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that a Single Judge of a High Court is bound by judicial discipline and decorum when faced with a prior decision from a coordinate bench (another Single Judge) on the same set of facts.
It was argued that if the subsequent judge disagreed with the earlier decision, the only proper judicial course was to refer the matter to a larger bench, not to issue a conflicting order.

statutes.act_name: Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960

cases.case_name: Lala Shri Bhagwan & Another v. Shri Ram Chand & Another
cases.principle: For considerations of judicial propriety and decorum, if a Single Judge is inclined to take the view that an earlier decision of the High Court needs to be reconsidered, they should refer the matter to a Division Bench or a larger Bench, rather than embarking upon that enquiry themselves.

cases.case_name: Eknath Shankarrao Mukkawar v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: When a judge disagrees with a decision of a coordinate court, the only judicial alternative, for reasons of judicial discipline and decorum, is to refer the matter to a larger bench and not to dispose of the case by taking a contrary view.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a Single Judge of a High Court disagrees with a prior decision of a coordinate bench, particularly on the same set of facts, judicial discipline and propriety require the judge to refer the matter to a larger bench for consideration rather than issuing a conflicting order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In our opinion, once the Single Judge, while deciding Criminal Writ Petition No. 4451/2022 formed an opinion that the judgment/order dated 16.12.2022 passed by the learned Single Judge was unsustainable and contrary to law, the matter should have been referred to a Division Bench/two-Judges Bench instead of passing a conflicting judgment in the same set of facts.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that if a learned Single Judge hearing a matter is inclined to take the view that the earlier decisions of the High Court, whether of a Division Bench or of a Single Judge, needed to be reconsidered, he should not embark upon that enquiry sitting as a Single Judge, but should refer the matter to a Division Bench or place it before the Chief Justice to constitute a larger Bench.

The rule that when there is a decision of a coordinate court, it is open to a learned Judge to differ from it, but in that case the only judicial alternative is to refer it to a larger bench and not to dispose of the appeal by taking a contrary view.

Rule 8 of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960, which states: 'If it shall appear to any Judge, either on the application of a party or otherwise, that an appeal or matter can be more advantageously heard by a Bench of two or more Judges, he may report to that effect to the Chief Justice who shall make such order thereon as he shall think fit.'
policy_considerations: Considerations of judicial propriety and decorum require a judge who disagrees with a coordinate bench to refer the matter to a larger bench.
Judicial discipline as well as decorum should suggest that referring a matter to a larger bench is the only course when a judge disagrees with a coordinate court's decision.

To avoid an 'incongruous situation where, in the same set of facts and one trial, there are two conflicting orders, one rejecting the challenge to framing of charge under Section 302 of IPC and other directing that the charge under Section 302 of IPC should not be framed.'
